newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean union boss says scrap law or face shutdown.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean union boss says scrap law or face shutdown.

text.p: South Korea's top strike leader on Wednesday issued an ultimatum to the government to scrap a new labour law within one week or face all-out work stoppages, including a public sector shutdown.
But the chairman of the ruling New Korea Party flatly rejected the demand.
Another party official suggested the ultimatum was a bluff and predicted strikes would soon fizzle.

Unions claimed almost 220,000 members were striking, including about 50,000 car workers, a similar number of metal workers and 80,000 staff from the giant Hyundai Group that makes everything from ships to computer chips.
The labour ministry put the number at less than 65,000. While car production remained crippled, most workers at major shipyards returned to their posts.

Kwon Young-kil, president of the outlawed Korean Confederation of Trade Unions, gave the government a deadline of midnight next Tuesday to repeal the labour bill that gives employers the right to lay off workers.
Unless the deadline was met the confederation would paralyse public services not already on strike, including subways, telecommunications and mints.
"If the Kim Young-sam government does not repeal the vicious labour law...we will enter the most intensive general strike struggle," he told a news conference.
General stoppages would begin immediately if state prosecutors carried out their threat to issue arrest warrants against union leaders, Kwon said.
On its own, the confederation would not be able to cripple public services.
While its 500,000 members have a grip on car and ship production, it shares power in public services with the much larger Federation of Korean Trade Uniions, which has 1.2 million members.
An earlier union attempt to briefly halt the Seoul subway failed completely after non-union drivers kept trains running.
The response by hospital workers and broadcasters to a strike call this week has been patchy.

However, joint action by the two union umbrella bodies, which guard their turf jealously, would produce a more powerful impact. Kwon said all organised labour groups would join forces starting next Monday.
Hours after Kwon's threat, New Korea Party chairman Lee Hong-ku told a news conference: "We will not change the law". He added that workers had nothing to fear.
"The majority of the Korean people will support the measures we have taken. Come spring the majority of labour unions will see there will be neither a reduction of wages nor major layoffs."
He was optimistic the economy, suffering from high costs that have exacerbated a trade deficit, would pick up later this year and "people will see we have made a right decision".
Lee Sang-deuk, chairman of the party's policy committee, told Reuters the ruling camp believed industrial action would soon burn itself out.
"There will be some union members that will try to prolong the strike but we believe the vast majority of workers will go back to work in the near future," he said.

In a move to lower the temperature, prosecutors said they would delay a decision to issue arrest warrants until Thursday. But a joint statement by the ministers of justice, interior and labour was uncompromising.
"If these illegal strikes continue, the government will have to take stern measures to secure industrial peace and keep legal order," it said.

In addition to car and ship production, confederation affiliates have a hold on the main subway lines in Seoul, major media outlets, hospitals, state-run telecommunications giant Korea Telecom and heavy industries.
They also control the unionised workforce at industrial giants Hyundai and Daewoo.
The federation is strongest among miners, electricity workers, railway workers, printers, port and postal workers, banking workers and various state industries, including the tobacco monopoly.
There is overlap between the bodies.
